title: Why Christmas Makes You Broke Until March
sources: National Retail Federation (NRF) 2025 Winter Holiday consumer survey (Prosper Insights & Analytics): average planned per-person holiday spend $890.49 in 2025, the second-highest in the survey's 23-year history, ~1.3% below the 2024 record of $901.99
NRF: U.S. holiday retail sales expected to surpass $1 trillion for the first time in 2025

Visualping analysis of 1,500+ tracked retail products (Oct-Cyber Monday 2025), as reported by CNBC (Nov 26, 2025): about one-third of Black Friday 'deals' showed no real discount vs Oct 27-Nov 17 prices; fake deals averaged ~37% above the item's true recent low price; WalletHub found 36% of sale items offered no savings; luggage had the highest share of fake deals (61%)

Adobe Analytics 2025 Holiday Shopping Report (released Jan 2026): Buy Now, Pay Later spending hit $20.0 billion during Nov 1-Dec 31, 2025, an all-time high, up 9.8% year-over-year; 82.2% of BNPL purchases made via smartphone

CFPB: in May 2024 issued an interpretive rule treating BNPL 'pay-in-4' loans like credit cards under Regulation Z; in May 2025 the CFPB said it will not enforce/reissue that rule, so BNPL currently faces lighter oversight than credit cards

Federal Reserve Bank of New York, Quarterly Report on Household Debt and Credit, Q4 2025 (released Feb 2026): credit card balances rose $44 billion in Q4 2025 to $1.28 trillion, up 5.5% year-over-year; total household debt rose $191 billion (1.0%) to $18.8 trillion

Federal Reserve Bank of New York, Household Debt and Credit, Q1 2026 (released May 12, 2026): credit card balances $1.25 trillion, down slightly quarter-over-quarter but up 5.9% year-over-year; total household debt $18.8 trillion (+0.1%)

Toy/kids-marketing figures (Statista; Amra & Elma industry compilation, 2025): U.S. baby & kids ad spend surpassed $1.5 billion in 2023 (excluding peak holiday-season spend); ~55% of toy purchases made online in 2025; licensed characters made up ~30% of 2025 toy sales

FTC, 'The ABCs at the FTC: Marketing and Advertising to Children' (FTC speeches/guidance) and FTC business guidance on advertising to children: children have limited ability to distinguish ads from entertainment, especially in digital/video media

LendingTree holiday debt survey (2,000+ U.S. consumers, results published Dec 2025/Jan 2026): 37% took on holiday debt, averaging $1,223 (up from $1,181 the prior year); of those with debt, 62% carried it on credit cards, 35% on BNPL loans, 32% on store cards; 40% pay interest of 20%+ APR; 63% expect repayment to take 3+ months
Illustrative math: $890.49 average spend x ~130 million U.S. households ≈ over $1 trillion in total holiday spending (rounded, per NRF household count and forecast)
Callback: credit card raccoon toll-booth analogy (ep02); Costco 'cheap stars get you in the door' analogy (ep36)

beats.text: It's March. Dave opens his banking app, and there it is. A leftover balance from Christmas.
Three hundred and twelve dollars. For a candle. A sweater nobody wears. And a roll of wrapping paper.
And here's the twist. Dave is not bad with money. The whole holiday season is built to end up right here, in his wallet, months later.
The ads. The fake discounts. The four little payments at checkout. Even his own kid's wish list.
Every part of the season quietly pulls a bit more out of his pocket, long after the tree hits the curb.
Today: how much people really spend, who profits from every dollar of it, and how to close out the year without opening a bill in March.
Let's start with the number Dave never actually adds up in his head.
Every year, the National Retail Federation asks shoppers what they plan to spend on the holidays.
For twenty twenty five, the average answer was eight hundred ninety dollars and forty nine cents. Per person.
That's gifts, food, decorations, cards, all of it. And it's the second highest number in the survey's twenty three year history.
Only about one percent below the record, set just one year before.
Multiply that by roughly a hundred thirty million U S households, and the whole country plans to spend over a trillion dollars, in about eight weeks.
Now, about those Black Friday signs screaming fifty percent off.
A twenty twenty five study tracked over fifteen hundred products, from October through Cyber Monday.
It found that about one in three of those Black Friday deals were not real discounts at all.
The price was the same, or even higher, than it had been just weeks earlier, in October.
Luggage was the worst offender. Sixty one percent of luggage deals were fake.
And even the fake ones tried to hide it. On average, that inflated 'sale' price was still thirty seven percent above the item's true recent low.

beats.chapter: Pay in Four, Regret in December
beats.text: So Dave sees a game console he can't quite afford. Then he sees four small payments instead of one big one.
That's buy now, pay later. Split the bill into four, often with no interest. Feels like nothing.
During the twenty twenty five holidays, shoppers used it for twenty billion dollars in purchases. An all time high.
That's almost ten percent more than the year before. Most of it tapped in on a phone, half asleep, at midnight.
And here's something worth knowing. Regulators walked back a rule that would have treated these plans exactly like credit cards. For now, buy now pay later plays by lighter rules.
The trick isn't the math. Four payments of twenty five dollars is still a hundred dollars. The trick is that it never feels like spending a hundred dollars all at once.

beats.chapter: Grandma's Layaway vs Dave's Four Payments
beats.text: Grandma used to do this completely differently. She'd put a toy on layaway.
Layaway means the store holds the item, and you pay it off first, a little at a time. You only take it home once it's fully paid.
Buy now pay later flips that around. You take the item home today, and pay it off after, in four pieces.
One method makes sure you can actually afford it, before you own it. The other one just bets you'll figure out the last payment somehow.
Grandma's version is slower, and way less exciting at checkout. It's also a lot harder to end up owing money you don't have.

beats.chapter: Your Balance Doesn't Know the Party's Over
beats.text: Meanwhile, Dave's credit card is quietly filling up.
The Federal Reserve Bank of New York tracks this every quarter. In the last three months of twenty twenty five, credit card balances jumped by forty four billion dollars.
That's one point two eight trillion dollars owed nationally, just on credit cards. Up five and a half percent from a year before.
By spring, the total balance had barely moved. It even dipped slightly. But it was still almost six percent higher than the spring before that.
In other words, the holiday spike doesn't just disappear in January. It quietly becomes the new normal balance.

beats.chapter: Marketed to Your Kids, Not to You
beats.text: Now here's the part that isn't really aimed at Dave at all. It's aimed at his kid.
Toy companies spend well over a billion and a half dollars a year on advertising, and that's before counting the holiday push itself.
More than half of all toys are now bought online, where a kid's video feed is basically one long wish list.
Characters from movies and games, the licensed stuff, now make up about thirty percent of all toy sales.
The Federal Trade Commission has flagged this exact problem: kids can't always tell where the show ends and the ad begins.
So the list taped to the fridge isn't just a kid being a kid. Some of it was built by a marketing team.
Most people think the holiday bill is a January problem, and then it's over. Nope.
A survey by LendingTree found thirty seven percent of shoppers took on actual debt to pay for the holidays.
Those people owed, on average, one thousand two hundred twenty three dollars. Up from the year before.
Most of that sits on credit cards, but about a third also carries buy now pay later debt on top of it.
And forty percent of these people are paying interest of twenty percent or more. That's not a small fee. That's a raccoon sized bite.
Almost two thirds said it would take three months or longer to pay it off. March isn't a coincidence. It's just the math.
So who wins, while Dave is still paying off Christmas in the spring?
Retailers win first. The industry expected holiday sales to cross one trillion dollars for the first time ever, in twenty twenty five.
Buy now pay later companies win next. They collect fees from stores on every split payment, plus late fees from shoppers who miss one.
And credit card companies win last, and longest. Every month Dave carries a balance, interest keeps compounding, quietly, in the background.
Nobody forced Dave to buy any of it. But almost every part of the system is built to make 'buy now' feel easier than 'wait and save'.

beats.chapter: How to Close the Year for Real
beats.text: So how does Dave avoid a March surprise next year? Remember, this is education, not advice.
One. Set the total gift budget in November, before a single ad shows up. Write the actual number down.
Two. Use cash, or a debit card, for gifts if you can. When the envelope is empty, the shopping stops.
Three. Suggest a Secret Santa, or a 'three gifts each' rule with family. Fewer presents, same amount of love.
Four. Treat buy now pay later like real debt, because it is. If you wouldn't split it across four credit cards, don't split it into four payments either.
Five. If you do carry a balance into January, pay that off before adding anything new. Don't let last Christmas share a bill with this year's birthday.
So let's recap.
One. Americans plan to spend about eight hundred ninety dollars each this holiday season, and roughly one in three Black Friday deals aren't even real discounts.
Two. Buy now pay later and credit card balances both spike in December, and for a lot of people, they don't fully come back down by spring.
Three. A November budget, cash envelopes, and fewer gifts beat almost every trick in the store.

youtube.hook: Why are you still paying off Christmas in March? Dave finds $312 of leftover holiday debt — and it's not bad luck, it's the business model. Dave checks his banking app in March and finds he's still paying off last Christmas: a candle, a sweater nobody wears, and wrapping paper. We break down why that happens: the real average holiday spend (NRF), how about one in three Black Friday 'deals' aren't real discounts, why buy-now-pay-later hit an all-time high last holiday season, how credit card balances spike in Q4 and don't fully come back down, how toy marketing targets kids directly, and why 37% of shoppers carry real debt into January. Then a practical, November-first way to close out the year without a March surprise.
